narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Demeter’s withdrawal threatens the growth that sustains mortals. Persephone returns, but the pomegranate binds her to time below as well. The hymn’s settlement concerns divine power, human survival, and reunion with a lasting limit.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “with joy and hastily sprang up for gladness. But he on his part secretly gave her sweet pomegranate seed to eat, taking care for himself that she might not remain continually with grave, dark-robed Demeter. Then Aidoneus the Ruler of Many openly got ready his deathless horses beneath the golden chariot.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The hymn's settlement says Persephone spends a third of the year below and two thirds with Demeter and the other gods.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Do not silently turn abduction and a constrained return into a freely chosen romance. Read the pomegranate within this hymn’s negotiations, while keeping later retellings separate.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Descent stories ask what part of the self can come back unchanged.
